title: The Carbon Cycle in 60 Seconds

endcard.line: Footage: NASA Goddard and Scientific Visualization Studio (public domain); Mostafameraji (CC0)

segments.say: The carbon in your body was once in the air. Before that, maybe in the sea, or in a rock. Carbon is always on the move.

anim.title: Into living things
items: Plants take carbon dioxide from the air

segments.say: Plants pull carbon dioxide out of the air and, with sunlight, turn it into sugar. Animals eat the plants, and the carbon moves on.
Breathing, rotting and burning send it back into the air. For thousands of years, the flows in and out roughly balanced.
The ocean is the biggest store of all. It soaks up carbon dioxide at its surface and slowly carries it down.
Some carbon goes deep. Ancient plants and plankton, buried for millions of years, became coal, oil and gas.
Burning those fuels returns, in a few centuries, carbon that took millions of years to store. Forests and oceans take up about half of it. The rest builds up in the air.
For Prelims: photosynthesis and the ocean are sinks; breathing, decay and burning are sources; fossil fuels are the fast leak.

sources: NASA Earth Observatory, 'The Carbon Cycle': fast and slow carbon cycles; photosynthesis, respiration, decay, ocean uptake; fossil fuels formed over millions of years
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Mauna Loa CO2 record: pre-industrial about 280 ppm; annual mean above 420 ppm by 2023–24
Global Carbon Project, Global Carbon Budget 2024: land and ocean sinks together take up roughly half of CO2 emissions from human activity
NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. on biosphere / NCERT Class 12 Biology ch. on ecosystems: carbon cycle

quiz.q: Which of these takes carbon dioxide OUT of the air?
quiz.why: Plants use carbon dioxide to make sugar.

quiz.q: What is the biggest active store of carbon?
quiz.why: The ocean soaks up and stores far more than the air.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of our CO2 do land and ocean sinks take up?
quiz.why: The rest builds up in the air.

reviewNote: Facts were read against NASA Earth Observatory's carbon-cycle feature, NOAA's Mauna Loa record and the Global Carbon Budget 2024. Footage is NASA visualisation and open sea. Moving facts: the CO2 level rises every year; 'over 420 ppm' stays true.
